sections.heading: Coming to you as I really am
sections.text: Eternal Father, you are better than I can understand or explain. I come to you without pretending. I am not only weak; I am sinful. I can say the right words quickly, but my heart is often slow to care, and my life is slow to change. So I bring my whole self to you. Do whatever mercy must do in me: humble me, wake me up, reshape me, and make me willing to be changed.
theological_themes: God is perfectly good, and honest confession begins by bringing the whole self before him without self-defense.
True repentance is more than words; it includes a softened heart and a changed life.

scripture_references.connection: David’s repentance shows that God is not looking for empty religious performance but for a heart broken open before him. This supports the prayer’s movement from verbal confession toward deeper inward contrition.
The prophet calls God’s people to return with their hearts, not merely with outward signs. That matches the prayer’s concern that confession must become real inward turning to God.

sections.heading: Asking you to show me sin for what it is
sections.text: Father, please strip away every disguise that makes sin look harmless, reasonable, or attractive. Let me see its ugliness clearly enough to hate it, turn from it, and run to you instead. I do not want to make peace with what damages my soul and dishonors you.
theological_themes: Sin deceives and must be exposed by God’s light.
Repentance includes learning to hate sin, not merely regretting its consequences.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist asks God to search and expose what is offensive in him and then lead him in the right way. That directly grounds this section’s request for God to uncover hidden sin and redirect the heart.
This passage warns that sin deceives and hardens the heart. It supports the prayer’s plea to stop seeing sin as harmless and to respond before the heart grows colder.

sections.heading: Admitting how I have used your gifts against you
sections.text: You gave me my mind, my body, my desires, my words, my time, and my strength. Too often I have turned those gifts into tools of rebellion. I have acted like your enemy while living on your kindness. I have used what belongs to you to serve what opposes you. Please give me grace to grieve this foolishness honestly. Teach me, not just in theory but deep down, that the road away from you is bitter, that sin’s path is miserable, and that leaving you means losing everything truly good.
theological_themes: Human abilities are gifts from God and can be misused in rebellion against him.
Sin is not freedom but misery, bondage, and loss.
Grace is needed even to mourn sin rightly.

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns believers not to present their bodies as instruments for sin but to offer themselves to God. This clearly supports the prayer’s confession that God-given capacities have been used as weapons of rebellion.
God describes his people’s departure from him as abandoning the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. That illuminates the prayer’s claim that turning from God is the loss of all real good.
This proverb teaches that the way of the faithless is ruinous. It supports the prayer’s request to understand that sinful paths are not merely forbidden but destructive.

sections.heading: Confessing that I sin against light and against your Spirit
sections.text: I have seen that your law is pure, beautiful, wise, and good. I have seen the quiet strength and joy of a life shaped by your commands. And still, day after day, I push aside what you have shown me and treat your words as if they were small. Your Spirit has been kind to warn me through Scripture, to unsettle me through your providence, and to draw me back in quiet ways I did not deserve. Yet I have often chosen my own schemes and cravings, even when they hurt me. I have resisted him, grieved him, and treated his holy patience lightly.
theological_themes: God’s law is good and beautiful, and disobedience is more serious when it is committed against known truth.
The Holy Spirit convicts, warns, and draws believers back to God.
Believers can grieve the Spirit by persistent sin and resistance.

scripture_references.connection: Paul affirms that God’s law is holy, righteous, and good. This supports the prayer’s confession that the problem is not with God’s commands but with the sinner who violates them.
This psalm praises the Lord’s instruction as wise, pure, and more desirable than riches. It grounds the prayer’s language about the beauty and happiness of a life governed by God’s word.
Paul explicitly warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit. This supports the prayer’s confession that sin is not merely rule-breaking but personal resistance against God’s gracious presence.

sections.heading: Asking for pardon, deeper repentance, and a clearer sight of the cross
sections.text: Father, I mourn these sins and ask you to forgive me. Do not let my repentance stay shallow or temporary. Work in me a grief that is honest and lasting: a grief that trembles before your holiness, yet still trusts your mercy; a grief that hates sin, yet keeps loving you; a grief that does not collapse into despair, because Christ has died for sinners like me. Through the tears of repentance, help me see the saving cross more clearly—its mercy brighter, its glory greater, and my Savior more precious than ever.
theological_themes: Forgiveness is sought from God for real guilt, not minimized wrongdoing.
Godly grief leads to repentance without despair because it rests in God’s mercy.
The cross of Christ is the believer’s hope and becomes clearer and more precious through true repentance.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches believers to confess sin truthfully and promises God’s faithful forgiveness and cleansing. This grounds the prayer’s request for pardon without denying the seriousness of sin.

Paul distinguishes godly grief from worldly grief: one leads to repentance and life, the other to death. This supports the prayer’s desire for sorrow that is deep, active, and hopeful rather than despairing.

Peter connects Christ’s bearing of sins on the cross with believers dying to sin and living to righteousness. This supports the prayer’s final movement from repentance to a clearer sight of the saving cross.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses very severe self-descriptions and asks God to “break” and “wound” the soul. I preserved the unsparing penitential force while rendering these as God’s merciful humbling, awakening, and reshaping rather than as a desire for harm for its own sake.

The line about provoking the Holy Spirit “to abandon me” can be read in ways that conflict with assurance and the Spirit’s sealing of believers. I rendered it as grieving and resisting the Spirit and treating his patience lightly, with the implied danger of losing comfort and help rather than God utterly forsaking someone who is in Christ.

The original mentions “startling providences” as divine warnings. Because interpreting specific events as direct messages from God can be pastorally risky, I kept the idea more modestly as God using providence to unsettle and turn the sinner back without claiming certainty about every hardship.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “my faculties” broadly as mind, body, desires, words, time, and strength—ordinary human capacities given by God and misused in sin.

I kept the original progression: adoration of God’s goodness, confession of inward slowness, request for sin to be exposed, admission of rebellion, recognition of the goodness of God’s law, confession of resisting the Spirit, plea for pardon, and longing to see the cross more clearly.

I rendered “godly grief that trembles and fears, yet ever trusts and loves” as repentance that takes God’s holiness seriously without falling into despair, because the original holds fear, trust, sorrow, and love together.
